The final revelations reframe Lucy's memories and the relationships surrounding the case, bringing the mystery to a conclusion that is both surprising and unsettling.

reviews.author: Amy Tintera
reviews.title: Listen For The Lie
reviews.summary: Lucy Chase returns to her hometown of Plumpton (funny name I know), Texas, after becoming the centre of a murder investigation. Years earlier, she was found wandering along a road covered in blood, with no memory of what happened to her best friend Savvy. Now, when a true-crime podcast revisits the unsolved case, Lucy finds herself dragged back into the mystery. Everyone seems to have an opinion about what happened, but with a town full of secrets and a narrator who cannot always trust her own memories, uncovering the truth becomes anything but simple.
reviews.spoilerCulpritReveal:
Matt, Savvy's husband, is ultimately revealed to be responsible for her death.

The revelation completely changes how the earlier events are understood. Lucy's blood-stained appearance and missing memories had made her seem guilty, while Matt had remained outside the centre of suspicion for much of the investigation.

The truth exposes the danger of accepting a convincing narrative without questioning who benefits from it. Lucy had spent years carrying the weight of a murder she did not commit, while the actual culprit had remained hidden behind the assumptions surrounding the case. 

The biggest misdirection in this case was never just Lucy's missing memory. It was how readily everyone else believed they already knew what had happened.
reviews.reviewText:
I went into this book expecting a fairly conventional murder mystery, but Lucy Chase made it anything but ordinary. One of my favourite things about this read was definitely the humour. Despite dealing with a murder investigation and some genuinely unsettling events, the book manages to be surprisingly funny without taking away from the mystery itself. And honestly, Lucy might just be one of my favourite main characters ever. Her sarcastic inner commentary reminded me of myself more than once, and I loved getting little glimpses into the way her brain works. I found myself looking forward to her reactions just as much as the actual investigation, which is probably a good indication of how much I enjoyed her character.

The podcast format was another detail I really enjoyed. It added a completely different layer to the story because we weren't just following an investigation; we were also getting to see how that investigation was being presented to everyone else. The interviews, public speculation and different accounts of what happened made me realise how easily a story can change depending on who's telling it. Everyone seemed to have their own version of Lucy, and I found it interesting how quickly people were willing to believe certain things about her without really knowing what had happened. It also made the whole situation feel a lot more personal because Lucy wasn't just trying to figure out the truth herself; she was dealing with an entire town that had practically decided her story for her.

The pacing was great, and I found myself changing suspects constantly. Every time I thought I had finally figured something out, another little detail would make me question everything all over again. I especially liked how the book played around with memory and perception. Lucy's missing memories made it difficult to know what to believe, and I loved that even the smallest interactions could leave me wondering whether there was something more going on. It made me realise just how much we rely on our own memories when trying to understand situations, and how unsettling it would be to have everyone else remember something that you simply couldn't.

If I had one criticism, it would be that a few of the revelations felt slightly convenient, and I would have liked certain parts of the mystery to be explored a little further. Nevertheless, this was such an entertaining read. I loved the balance between humour and suspense, and I think Lucy is what really makes the book stand out. I would genuinely love to read another book featuring her because, at this point, I'm probably just as interested in following her thoughts as I am in solving the actual murder.
reviews.spoilerEvidence:
For most of the investigation, Lucy is positioned as the obvious suspect. She was found covered in blood, cannot remember the night Savvy died, and has spent years being judged by a town convinced she murdered her best friend.

However, the investigation gradually reveals that the story everyone has accepted is not the complete truth.

The focus eventually shifts towards Matt, whose relationship with Savvy and involvement in the events surrounding her death become central to the mystery. The details of their marriage expose a much darker situation than the version of events initially presented to the public.

The podcast, conflicting testimonies and Lucy's fragmented memories all contribute to the gradual dismantling of the original theory. What initially appears to be a straightforward case against Lucy turns into a revelation about how easily the wrong person can become the centre of an entire town's suspicion.

clues.detailedAnalysis: This becomes the foundation of the entire investigation. The physical circumstances make Lucy appear guilty, but the absence of reliable memories means that appearances cannot be treated as proof.

reviews.finalVerdict: A witty, unpredictable murder mystery with an unforgettable narrator, plenty of suspicious characters and just enough twists to keep you questioning everyone.
reviews.whatIThought: I spent most of the book questioning whether Lucy's missing memories were hiding something much darker than she realised. I suspected that the people around her knew considerably more than they were letting on, especially given how quickly the town seemed to settle on its own version of events. I also kept wondering whether the podcast was genuinely trying to solve the case or simply using Lucy's past to create a more entertaining story.

reviews.recommendedFor: Readers who enjoy psychological thrillers, isolated settings, unreliable characters, and stories that blur the line between fiction and reality.
reviews.reviewText: The premise immediately grabbed me: a negative book review leading to a real-life nightmare is such a clever setup. However it felt a bit like the start of a dramatic movie rather than psychological thriller so I dived into this book with more a mindset which left me rather unprepared for the plots and twisty writing. The isolated beach house also adds to this creating an unsettling atmosphere, and the story keeps you questioning.I liked how the book plays with the line between fiction and reality. However I think by the end it left more questions than answers and kept me wanting more from the book. The fast pacing and constant reveals make it an easy thriller to get pulled into, although the number of twists can sometimes feel a little over-the-top. Overall, it’s a tense, unpredictable read with a memorable premise. It may stretch believability at times, but it knows how to keep the suspense going.
reviews.author: Taylor Adams
reviews.leadQuote: "One harmless review turns into a nightmare."
reviews.spoilerEvidence: Emma’s one-star review initially points towards H.G. Kane as the person behind her nightmare. However, Kane is revealed to be Howard Grosvenor Kline, who physically attacks Emma. The real mastermind is Deek, her seemingly helpful neighbour, who orchestrated the events and used Howard to carry out his plan. The manuscript and Deek’s suspicious behaviour take on a new meaning once his involvement is exposed.
reviews.summary: While house-sitting at a remote beach home, Emma Carpenter leaves a scathing review of a horror novel by H. G. Kane. The author responds by stalking her, turning Emma’s quiet retreat into a fight for survival. With only her dog Laika and distant, rather strange neighbour Deek to rely on, Emma must figure out who is behind the attacks and why.
reviews.favoriteMoment: The moment Deek’s apparent role as Emma’s helpful neighbour turns sinister. It completely changes how his earlier actions read and makes the story’s final twist especially unsettling.
reviews.title: The Last Word
reviews.spoilerCulpritReveal: Deek, whose real identity is Deacon Cowl, reveals that he planned the ordeal to create a sensational real-life story and revive his failing writing career. He manipulated Emma’s trust and turned her nightmare into material for his own ambitions. Howard was the attacker, but Deek was the mastermind behind it all.
reviews.whatIThought: I suspected H. G. Kane was behind the attacks, but I thought Deek might be helping him or hiding something about the house. I expected Emma’s review to be the reason she was targeted, but I didn’t anticipate how deeply the events were connected to the people around her.
reviews.finalVerdict: A clever, fast-paced thriller with enough twists to keep you guessing.

reviews.whatActuallyHappened: H. G. Kane is Howard, the homeowner’s son, and he attacks Emma after her review. Emma survives and kills him, but the danger isn’t over. Deek later reveals that he orchestrated the attack to create a sensational story and revive his writing career. He drugs Emma and tries to stage her death, but she escapes and reaches the police. The ending also reveals that Emma’s husband Shawn is alive; their baby daughter died in a car accident, and Emma had been isolating herself in grief.

reviews.summary: After years of working in other people’s homes, Millie finally has a house of her own with her husband, Enzo, and their two children. But their fresh start in a quiet Long Island neighbourhood quickly turns unsettling. Their neighbours are strange, Enzo starts acting suspiciously, and the family discovers that their new home may be hiding something. When a neighbour is found dead, Millie’s seemingly perfect life spirals into a mystery filled with secrets, lies, and unexpected suspects.
reviews.spoilerEvidence:
Jonathan Lowell’s murder appears to implicate Enzo, while Ada’s confession reveals that she had attacked Jonathan after discovering his disturbing secret involving Nico. However, Ada’s attack was not the fatal one. The final revelation exposes a second, unexpected act of violence that changes the entire interpretation of the case.

Martha, the housemaid, returned to the Lowell home to steal jewellery as she tried to escape her abusive husband. When Jonathan caught her and threatened to expose her, she killed him with a letter opener. Because Jonathan was already wounded, the earlier events made it difficult to establish who had actually caused his death. Martha escaped, while Suzette ultimately took the blame.
reviews.spoilerCulpritReveal:
Martha’s motive was a combination of desperation and self-preservation. She wanted the jewellery to help her escape her abusive marriage, but Jonathan’s threat to report her put that plan at risk. Rather than face the consequences, she killed him and fled.

The most important twist is that Ada wounded Jonathan, but Martha caused his fatal injury. Enzo’s apparent guilt and Suzette’s confession further complicate the investigation, allowing Martha to remain hidden. The epilogue reveals that the housemaid who seemed peripheral to the mystery was actually the person responsible for the final, deadly act.
reviews.recommendedFor: Readers who enjoy unreliable narrators and multiple twists.    Fans of domestic thrillers where ordinary homes conceal disturbing secrets.    Readers who enjoy endings that make them reconsider earlier clues.
reviews.favoriteMoment: The most chilling moment is the final revelation about Martha. Just when the mystery appears solved and the family can move on, the epilogue reveals that the person who seemed least threatening was responsible for the fatal injury.
reviews.reviewText: I was honestly excited to see Millie and Enzo again, but this time, instead of dealing with another wealthy family’s problems, we get to see Millie navigating her own suburban nightmare. And somehow, the neighbours manage to be just as suspicious as the people she used to work for. The beginning does a good job of building that uncomfortable feeling that something is seriously wrong. Between the overly involved neighbours, Enzo’s suspicious behaviour, and the strange discoveries around the house, there’s plenty to keep you questioning everyone. I also liked that the story shifts its focus towards Millie’s family, giving us a different side of her life. I get a bit emotional saying this but this book truly felt like a tribute back to the original. There are so many secrets and suspicious characters it just all pulls back to the first book and reminds me of why I was so addicted before. The twists are entertaining, but some of the reveals feel more shocking than genuinely satisfying, and I found myself questioning a few of the characters’ decisions.Overall, it was an entertaining return to the series, especially for someone already invested in Millie’s story. It has the classic combination of short chapters, family secrets, and last-minute revelations, absolutely amazing read thank you Fredia.
reviews.whatIThought: I suspected Enzo was hiding something much worse than he was letting on, especially with his unexplained disappearances and the suspicious evidence surrounding him. I also thought the neighbours were involved in something together, and that the seemingly perfect suburban life was hiding a much darker reality. I expected the murder mystery to connect everyone somehow, but I definitely didn't predict how many layers the truth would have.
reviews.whatActuallyHappened:
Enzo initially appears to be the killer, but the truth is much more complicated. Ada reveals that she confronted Jonathan Lowell after discovering what he had done to Nico and attacked him. Suzette later falsely confesses to Jonathan’s murder to protect herself from exposure for her own involvement in his crimes.

The final twist reveals that Martha, the housemaid, delivered the fatal injury after finding Jonathan wounded and confronting him while stealing jewellery. She feared the consequences of being caught and wanted to escape her abusive husband. Meanwhile, Suzette takes the blame, and Martha remains free.

Just when the mystery seems solved, the ending reveals that the person who appeared to be on the sidelines was hiding the biggest secret of all.

reviews.whatActuallyHappened:
The revelations surrounding Douglas, Wendy, and Millie's involvement turn the situation into something far more complicated than it first appears. The story challenges your assumptions about who is really in danger and who is hiding the truth.

Although the twists added some excitement, they didn't completely make up for the slower parts of the book for me. The ending had its moments, but overall, I was left thinking that the first book had been the stronger read.
reviews.spoilerEvidence: The central deception revolves around Douglas Garrick's account of his wife, Wendy, and the disturbing circumstances surrounding her confinement. Millie's discoveries gradually expose the gap between the story she is told and what is actually happening. The novel uses shifting assumptions about victimhood, control, and trust to make the reader reconsider who is manipulating whom.
reviews.author: Fredia Mcfadden
reviews.reviewText: After absolutely loving the first book, I went into The Housemaid's Secret with pretty high expectations. Unfortunately, this sequel didn't quite deliver the same excitement for me. McFadden's writing is still simple and easy to fly through, but the pacing felt slower than I expected. The premise was intriguing, and there were definitely moments that made me curious, but I never felt as hooked as I did with the first book. I wanted that constant urge to read just one more chapter, and this time, it was missing.While there were some interesting twists, the overall experience felt a little underwhelming. Maybe my expectations were simply too high after the first book, but I wanted more suspense and a stronger reason to keep turning the pages. It was entertaining enough, but it didn't leave the same impression on me. I'll still give Millie another chance, though, because apparently, I haven't learnt my lesson yet.
reviews.recommendedFor: - Fans of Freida McFadden and The Housemaid. - Readers who enjoy domestic suspense, suspicious characters, and secrets hidden behind wealthy households. - Anyone looking for a relatively quick, accessible thriller rather than a complex, slow-burn mystery.
reviews.favoriteMoment: The moments when Millie discovers the bloodstained nightclothes and realises that something is seriously wrong with Wendy. The contrast between Douglas's seemingly perfect life and the disturbing secrets inside his penthouse creates an unsettling atmosphere. It was the kind of setup that made me curious, even if the book didn't keep me hooked the entire way through.
reviews.whatIThought: I expected the mystery surrounding Wendy's confinement to be the main focus, with Douglas hiding something far more sinister than he initially let on. I was ready for a complicated web of lies, shocking revelations, and a twist that would completely change how I viewed the characters.
marginaliaNotes: Why is every rich household Millie enters a walking red flag? Girl, can we get ONE normal employer?
Trust absolutely nobody. Not the husband, not the explanations, not even my own theories at this point.
reviews.finalVerdict: A promising, easy-to-read thriller with intriguing secrets and a few good twists, but one that lacked the pacing and addictive pull that made the first book so memorable.

reviews.spoilerCulpritReveal: Theo’s motive was revenge. He wanted Gabriel to suffer for having an affair with Kathy, but his plan ultimately led to Gabriel’s death and Alicia’s silence. When Alicia realized who Theo was, she documented the truth, eventually exposing him.
reviews.finalVerdict: A masterpiece with the best story writing concepts all deliciously combined into one delightful experience
reviews.reviewText:
I absolutely LOVE this book, like everyone else in the thriller community, what an amazing read. The Silent Patient is built around the mystery of Alicia’s silence, but its real strength is how it makes the reader question Theo while simultaneously trusting him. It makes for a perfectly suspenseful read while making me think through every interaction again and again. His investigation into Alicia felt so convincing because we experience everything through his perspective, making his personal obsession so easy to overlook.

I love the use of Alicia’s diary, gradually revealing pieces of her life before Gabriel’s death, it gave so much essence to Alicia as a character even without her actually ever communicating. The biggest trick is the timeline: Theo makes the reader believe his personal story is happening alongside Alicia’s treatment, when his story actually takes place years earlier.

Its beautifully revealed using Alicia’s final diary entry exposing the truth and turning the entire narrative on its head. What an amazing experience this book was its almost admirable how brilliantly it was created. It was truly mind boggling throughout and kept me entertained but the ending could've done better, it all felt a bit anti climatic and too easy to digest I just wanted something more.

The climax occurs when Andrew traps Millie inside the soundproofed attic, intending to starve and break her as he did with Nina. reviews.reviewText: I actually borrowed this book from a friend, not entirely convinced I wanted to commit to the series, but HOLY, I have learnt to absolutely love Freida McFadden through this read. This was definitely not an academic read in any way; it was purely to satisfy my guilty pleasures. Having read a few of her books and knowing just how notorious she is for her addictive "popcorn thrillers", this was the perfect combination of her fast-paced storytelling and wonderfully simple writing. Once I started, I genuinely could not put it down. There was always something to look forward to, and honestly, I think that's one of the best things about McFadden's books. It never really felt like I was reading; I was just constantly caught up in the story. Every chapter somehow found a permanent little corner in my head because I was always coming up with theories, questioning characters and trying to figure out what would happen next. I hold this book particularly dear to my heart because it was the inspiration behind creating this website in the first place. So, if you've read The Housemaid, I really hope you'll share your theories, suspicions and favourite moments here. I would absolutely love to hear what everyone else made of it!
reviews.summary: A desperate ex-con lands a live-in maid position with a wealthy, manic family on Long Island, only to discover the attic door locks from the exterior and the pristine husband might not be the saint he appears to be.

### Dissecting the Narrative • The Forensic Autopsy

I chose *Stone Blind* because I already knew about Medusa’s assault and wanted to explore the story beyond the version of the myth I had grown up hearing. I knew she was transformed into a Gorgon, that Perseus eventually hunted her, and that her head became a weapon. What I wanted to understand was how the story had reached that point and, more importantly, what Medusa’s experience of it all had actually been.

What I found particularly interesting was how Natalie Haynes uses different perspectives to reveal the injustice behind the myth. My obsession with true crime has made me increasingly interested in how stories are told, how evidence and perspectives shape public opinion, and how often victims are judged while those responsible escape the same scrutiny. I see so many real-world examples where the person who has been wronged ends up being questioned, blamed or forgotten. Seeing something similar unfold in Medusa’s story made it feel much more human and real to me. Through Medusa’s perspective, she is no longer just a terrifying figure; she is a young woman with sisters, relationships and a life that is taken away from her. Through Athene’s perspective, we see how Medusa is transformed and punished for Poseidon’s actions, while Poseidon himself does not face the same consequences. That contrast made the injustice even harder to ignore.

The shifting perspectives also changed how I viewed Perseus. I had always understood him as the hero of the myth, but Haynes makes us look beyond that familiar label and consider the story from the perspective of the person being hunted. We see how Medusa becomes a target in someone else's heroic journey, with her own fears and humanity pushed aside. It made me question how easily history turns one person into a hero and another into a monster, simply because of whose perspective gets remembered.

By the end, I felt that I had almost been introduced to an entirely different Medusa. I already knew what had happened to her, but I had never considered what it might have felt like to live through it. I found that especially difficult to separate from the injustices I see around me. Medusa deserved to be remembered for more than her appearance, her powers, or the fear she inspired. She deserved to have her story told as a person, not just as a monster. Stone Blind makes a meaningful effort to give Medusa that humanity, and I hope it inspires other readers to look beyond the familiar myth and research the stories and perspectives we may have overlooked.

nonFictionBooks.tagline: A brilliant, feminist retelling of Medusa’s myth that questions who gets called a monster—and who gets remembered as a hero.
nonFictionBooks.author: Natalie Haynes
nonFictionBooks.summary: In Stone Blind, Natalie Haynes retells the myth of Medusa, a mortal girl raised by her immortal Gorgon sisters. After Poseidon assaults Medusa in Athene’s temple, Athene punishes Medusa by transforming her into a Gorgon whose gaze turns living beings to stone. Forced into isolation, Medusa’s story eventually collides with Perseus’s quest to claim a Gorgon’s head. Through shifting perspectives and sharp humour, the novel challenges the traditional portrayal of Medusa as a monster and Perseus as a hero.

nonFictionBooks.title: Gray After Dark
nonFictionBooks.reviewText:
Honestly wasn't prepared for just how stressful this read would become. One of my favourite things about Gray After Dark was the setting. There's something particularly unsettling about the idea of being stranded in the middle of an enormous wilderness, completely cut off from the rest of the world. The cabin, the surrounding forest and the sheer distance from civilisation create an atmosphere that makes everything feel so much more threatening.

Miley was definitely one of the strongest parts of the book for me. I loved how her background as an athlete actually became an important part of her survival rather than just being an interesting detail about her character. Her discipline, determination and ability to think strategically all come into play. What I found particularly interesting, though, was that her biggest struggle wasn't just physical. Her guilt surrounding her mother's death had clearly affected the way she viewed herself, and I liked how her personal journey developed alongside the survival storyline.

The dynamic between Miley and Mary was another part I really enjoyed. At first, I wasn't entirely sure what to make of Mary, and I found myself constantly questioning how much she knew and whether she could actually be trusted. Watching their relationship develop was particularly interesting because it added another emotional layer to a story that could otherwise have focused entirely on escaping the cabin. Their eventual alliance became one of the most important parts of the book.

I also really appreciated the alternating perspectives. Being able to follow Miley's experience while also seeing Brent and Wes trying to find her created a completely different kind of tension. Every time the story switched away from Miley, I found myself wanting to get straight back to her chapters, but I also loved seeing the search unfold. Knowing that people were getting closer while Miley was still trapped made the whole situation feel even more urgent.

If I had one criticism, it would be that certain parts of the story felt quite drawn out, particularly as Miley's captivity continued. I understand why the author took the time to establish just how difficult her situation was, but there were moments when I was desperately waiting for something to change. Nevertheless, the payoff was worth it. This was such an intense read, and I think the combination of survival, psychological tension and character development made it stand out.

nonFictionBooks.summary: After an accident sidelines her Olympic ambitions, Miley takes a job at a remote mountain lodge in Idaho. However, a morning run turns into a nightmare when she is abducted by Fred and his son Hamish and taken to an isolated cabin. There, she encounters Mary, another woman held captive for years. As Miley struggles to escape, her friend Brent and lodge employee Wes begin searching for her, refusing to accept that she has simply disappeared. Through alternating perspectives, the novel explores survival, psychological control, trauma and the determination to reclaim one's identity.

actionItems: Pay attention to the choices you are making now instead of constantly comparing them to hypothetical alternatives.
nonFictionBooks.reviewText:
Dark Matter takes a huge sci-fi concept and makes it surprisingly personal. The multiverse isn't just used as a way to create increasingly complicated worlds; it becomes a way of exploring regret, ambition, identity, and the choices that shape a person's life.

The science is definitely a major part of the appeal, but the emotional side is what gives the story weight. Jason's desperation to get back to Daniela and Charlie keeps the story grounded even when the plot becomes increasingly impossible.

I also liked how the book plays with the idea of meeting versions of yourself who made completely different decisions. It turns the familiar “what if I had chosen differently?” question into an actual reality. The pacing is extremely quick, with Crouch constantly throwing another problem or revelation into the story, which makes it very easy to keep reading.

What stayed with me most is the question underneath all the science: if there are countless versions of your life, how do you decide which one is actually yours?
nonFictionBooks.summary: This book is mind numbingly perfect, I'm in no way a sci-fi reader but this book was so well written, it had such a great, unique plot and is probably my most memorable read. Jason Dessen is abducted and wakes up in a reality where his life has completely changed. His wife and son are gone, while an alternate version of Jason has become a brilliant physicist and achieved something impossible. Jason must navigate alternate realities to find his way back to the family and life he remembers.
keyTakeaways: Your choices don't just change your circumstances; they shape who you become.
An imagined alternative life can look perfect from a distance without actually being better.

heroConfig.headline: “ANOTHER BOOK. ANOTHER SUSPECT.”
heroConfig.bioParagraph1: Welcome to my private archive. I am a student who began reading thrillers under the innocent premise of wanting to know what happened next. I continued reading them because, apparently, I enjoy distrusting fictional strangers in locked rooms at 2:00 AM while ignoring my homework.
heroConfig.bioParagraph2: This space functions as my personal reading journal crossed with a vintage police blotter. Here, every domestic dispute is a potential felony, every housekeeper has an ulterior motive, and every charming husband is guilty until proven deceased.

currentlyReading.title: Tuesdays With Morrie
currentlyReading.nonThrillerThoughts: I'm sure this book will make me cry, a start to a new book is always exciting but this particular one remained on my wishlist because I knew it would make me emotional. I hold this new read dear to heart, my first book suggestion from my dad, who thought the obsession was rather silly. So far it has made me yearn for a relationship like this for someone to be so ready to guide me like Morrie is and I hope I continue the book as much as I do right now.

additionalBooks.currentTheory: I loved the series, and I’m hoping I’ll love the book even more. I do hope the story feels more carefully planned and put together, as books often do. This is a sensitive topic, so I know I need to approach the review thoughtfully and be mindful of how I express my opinions. Thankfully, I haven’t experienced anything like what the story explores, and I don’t want to speak as though I understand something I haven’t lived through. If anything I write comes across as insensitive or based on false assumptions, that’s not my intention. With that said, I’m hoping this read won’t leave me permanently scarred.

aboutConfig.bioParagraph3: I'm definitely the kind of reader who suspects everyone, overanalyses the smallest details and changes theories approximately five times before finishing a book. I have a habit of mentally investigating characters instead of simply enjoying the story, and I rarely trust an innocent-looking neighbour. Between procrastinating with one more chapter, collecting books faster than I can read them and trying to balance reading with preboard revision, there's always another story waiting on my shelf.
